subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If A, B are two independent events in a sample space S, then prove that Aᶜ, Bᶜ are independent.

mark_split.label: Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ = (A ∪ B)ᶜ, so P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ) = 1 − P(A ∪ B)
Expand P(A ∪ B) and use independence

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove that the complements of independent events are independent — the set identity you start from, where independence is used, and the factoring at the end.
insider_note: The proof is one chain of equalities; the mark is in the two reasons written beside it — De Morgan at the start and "A, B independent" in the middle.

steps.label: Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ = (A ∪ B)ᶜ
steps.margin_note: First mark. "Neither A nor B" is the complement of "A or B", so its probability is 1 − P(A ∪ B).

lines.text: Given A, B are independent, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B).
P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ) = P((A ∪ B)ᶜ) = 1 − P(A ∪ B)

recall.must_convey: That Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ is the complement of A ∪ B, so P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).
accept: A complement intersection B complement is the complement of A union B so its probability is one minus P A union B
start with de morgan, neither is one minus the union
P of A complement and B complement equals one minus P of A union B
A complement intersection B complement ante A union B complement, 1 minus P of union
heard_as: one minus P A union B

steps.why: There is no direct formula for an intersection of complements; De Morgan turns it into a union, which the addition theorem can expand.
common_mistakes: Assuming P(Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ) = P(Aᶜ)P(Bᶜ) — that is what is to be proved.

steps.label: Expand and use independence
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Addition theorem on P(A ∪ B), then replace P(A ∩ B) by P(A)·P(B) — write "A, B independent" beside that line.

recall.must_convey: That P(A ∪ B) is expanded by the addition theorem and P(A ∩ B) replaced by P(A)·P(B) because A, B are independent, giving 1 − P(A) − P(B) + P(A)P(B).
accept: expand the union as P A plus P B minus P A intersection B and replace the intersection by P A times P B since they are independent
one minus P A minus P B plus P A P B using independence
addition theorem then independence gives one minus P A minus P B plus the product
union ni addition theorem tho expand chesi, independent kabatti intersection ni product ga rayali
heard_as: one minus P A minus P B

steps.why: This is the only place the hypothesis is used; without independence the product would not appear and the factoring in the next step would be impossible.
common_mistakes: Dropping the sign on P(A ∩ B) when removing the bracket.
Not naming independence as the reason for the product.

steps.label: Factor and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. 1 − P(A) − P(B) + P(A)P(B) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)). Then say what that equality means.

lines.text: ⇒ Aᶜ, Bᶜ are independent. Hence proved.

recall.must_convey: That the expression factors as (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)) = P(Aᶜ)P(Bᶜ), so Aᶜ and Bᶜ satisfy the product rule and are independent.
accept: factor it as one minus P A times one minus P B which is P A complement times P B complement so the complements are independent
the expression factors into the product of the two complement probabilities hence proved
P of A complement and B complement equals the product so they are independent
factor cheste P A complement into P B complement, so complements independent
heard_as: one minus P A times one minus P B
P A complement times P B complement

steps.why: Independence of two events MEANS their intersection probability equals the product; showing that for Aᶜ, Bᶜ is the whole proof.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the factored form without saying it proves independence.
